source: Structural analysis of the allosteric sites of EAAT1 and ASCT2 suggests that two non-conserved residues in EAAT1 (e.g., F136, and I237) significantly contribute to the UCPH-101 interaction, while other binding site residues that are less critical for binding are conserved between EAAT1 and ASCT2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

source: Conversely, some residues are not fully conserved. Most notably, Y127 and M271 correspond to F136 and I237 in ASCT2, affecting the shape and polarity of the binding site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the chemical properties of the amino acid residues.

claim: Molecular docking of UCPH-101 to the putative allosteric site of ASCT2 fails using multiple approaches.

claim: Glutamate-induced EAAT1 anion current was inhibited in a concentration-dependent manner by UCPH-101.
source: As reported previously (Erichsen et al., 2010; Abrahamsen et al., 2013; Jensen et al., 2009), glutamate-induced EAAT1 anion current was inhibited in a concentration-dependent manner by UCPH-101 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings shown in the figure.

claim: At low [UCPH-101] (2 μM) onset of inhibition was slow with complete inhibition reached only after several seconds.
source: At low [UCPH-101] (2 μM) (Figure 3A, red trace) onset of inhibition was slow with complete inhibition reached only after several seconds.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the time course of current recordings shown in the figure.

claim: The apparent Ki for UCPH-101 was essentially independent of the glutamate concentration.
source: In agreement with the expectation of a non-competitive inhibition mechanism, the apparent Ki was essentially independent of the glutamate concentration (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from dose-response curves shown in the figure.

claim: Anion currents were fully inhibited at all membrane potentials by UCPH-101.
source: As expected, anion currents were fully inhibited at all membrane potentials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from voltage-dependence experiments shown in the figure supplement.

claim: EAAT1 anion currents show rapid rise of the current after glutamate application within the time resolution afforded by solution exchange (5–10 ms).
source: EAAT1 anion currents (Figure 4A) and transport currents (Figure 4E) show rapid rise of the current after glutamate application within the time resolution afforded by solution exchange (5–10 ms).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from rapid solution exchange experiments shown in the figure.

claim: The rise of the current is followed by rapid decay of a transient current component to the steady state.
source: The rise of the current is followed by rapid decay of a transient current component to the steady state, as demonstrated previously (Grewer et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an experimental observation consistent with previous studies.

claim: The transient phase of the current was previously assigned to steps associated with the glutamate translocation reaction.
source: This transient phase of the current was previously assigned to steps associated with the glutamate translocation reaction (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation from cited literature.

claim: After pre-incubation and in the continuous presence of UCPH-101, both transient and steady-state current amplitude were reduced in a dose-dependent manner.
source: After pre-incubation and in the continuous presence of UCPH-101, both transient and steady-state current amplitude were reduced in a dose-dependent manner, as expected (Figure 4B and F, currents were fully eliminated at 40 μM UCPH-101), but at concentrations close to the apparent Ki, the decay of the current was also slowed (Figure 4D, τ=11 ± 1.3, 16±2.1, 20±2.1 ms, at 0, 0.2, and 2 μM UCPH-101, respectively).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from rapid solution exchange experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Currents were fully eliminated at 40 μM UCPH-101.
source: After pre-incubation and in the continuous presence of UCPH-101, both transient and steady-state current amplitude were reduced in a dose-dependent manner, as expected (Figure 4B and F, currents were fully eliminated at 40 μM UCPH-101), but at concentrations close to the apparent Ki, the decay of the current was also slowed (Figure 4D, τ=11 ± 1.3, 16±2.1, 20±2.1 ms, at 0, 0.2, and 2 μM UCPH-101, respectively).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the figure.

claim: The reduction of the decay rate of the transient current indicates a slowing of the translocation reaction in the presence of UCPH-101.
source: The reduction of the decay rate of the transient current indicates a slowing of the translocation reaction in the presence of UCPH-101.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the kinetic data.

claim: UCPH-101 application in the absence of glutamate did not induce any currents.
source: In contrast to competitive inhibitors, UCPH-101 application in the absence of glutamate did not induce any currents, as expected for non-competitive inhibitors, which are not known to be able to block the glutamate transporter leak anion conductance (Figure 4C and G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the figure.

claim: Upon removal of glutamate, recovery of the transient current upon glutamate application in a second pulse was relatively slow, with a time constant of 95±4 ms.
source: Upon removal of glutamate, recovery of the transient current upon glutamate application in a second pulse was relatively slow, with a time constant of 95±4 ms, most likely reflecting the turnover time of the transporter, which has to recycle its binding sites to outward-facing, after passing through a whole transport cycle.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from paired-pulse experiments.

claim: At 0.2 μM UCPH-101 recovery of the transient current after glutamate removal occurred with a time constant of 115±11 ms.
source: At 0.2 μM UCPH-101 recovery of the transient current after glutamate removal occurred with a time constant of 115±11 ms, as quantified in Figure 4F and H.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from paired-pulse experiments shown in the figure.

claim: UCPH-101 does not significantly slow the recovery rate of the transient current.
source: Therefore, it appears that UCPH-101 does not significantly slow the recovery rate of the transient current.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic measurements.

claim: At low concentrations (<1 μM) UCPH-101 binding to EAAT1 and unbinding are very slow, with time constant of 10 s for binding, and 100 s for dissociation.

evidence: This is a kinetic parameter from cited literature.

claim: Within the time course of the paired-pulse experiment (1.4 s), UCPH-101-bound and -unbound transporter populations do not interconvert.
source: Thus, within the time course of the paired-pulse experiment (1.4 s), UCPH-101-bound and -unbound transporter populations do no interconvert, and the time course of current recovery, thus, reflects that of the UCPH-101-free state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the slow binding/unbinding kinetics.

claim: The time constant of the responses were biphasic and required fitting with two exponential components.

claim: UCPH-101 not only inhibits current amplitude, but also slows current kinetics and serine exchange turnover.

claim: ASCT2 is an amino acid exchanger.

claim: ASCT2 amino acid exchange is electroneutral at equilibrium.

evidence: This is a mechanistic property observed in the experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Upon rapid removal of extracellular amino acid, transient outward current was observed.

evidence: This is an experimental observation from rapid solution exchange experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Na+ apparent binding affinity to the apo-form of the ASCT2 transporter is high (Km < 1 mM).

evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental conditions and known properties of the transporter.

claim: Alanine and serine exchange was previously reported to be rapid in ASCT2.
